when.en: Anything finished: *أَمْسِ* yesterday, *الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِيَ* last week.
Arabic has one past. It covers I wrote, I have written and I did write.

how.en: Start from the dictionary form, which is he: *كَتَبَ* he wrote. Swap the ending for the person. The ending alone says who, so the pronoun is optional: *كَتَبْتُ* is I wrote.

tip.en: *ـتُ* I, *ـتَ* you to a man, *ـتِ* you to a woman. Same letters, different vowel: the ḥarakāt matter here.

when.en: Now, and things done usually: *كُلَّ يَوْمٍ* every day, *الْآنَ* now.
It is also the base for the future, for orders, and for most negatives.

how.en: A prefix says who (*أَ* I, *تَ* you or she, *يَ* he or they, *نَ* we), and some persons add an ending too (*ـِينَ* you to a woman, *ـُونَ* you all and they). The middle vowel belongs to the verb: *يَكْتُبُ*, *يَشْرَبُ*, *يَجْلِسُ*. Learn it with the verb.

ex.en: What are you studying? (to a woman)

tip.en: *تَكْتُبُ* is both you (to a man) and she writes. The sentence tells you which.

when.en: Things to come: *غَدًا* tomorrow, *الْأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِمَ* next week.

how.en: Join *سَ* to the front of the present: *سَأَكْتُبُ* I will write. The separate word *سَوْفَ* means the same and is a little more formal: *سَوْفَ أَكْتُبُ*.

tip.en: Will not is a different word: *لَنْ*, with no *سَ*. See its card.

when.en: Telling someone to do something: open, sit, come.

how.en: Take the you form of the present and drop the prefix: *تَجْلِسُ* becomes *اِجْلِسْ* sit. If what is left starts with two consonants, add *اِ* or *اُ* in front (*اُكْتُبْ*). The last vowel goes silent.

tip.en: Don't do it is not an imperative: it is *لَا* with the short present, *لَا تَكْتُبْ*.

when.en: Saying no about now or usually: I don't know, she doesn't eat meat.

how.en: Put *لَا* before the present. Nothing else changes: *أَعْرِفُ* I know, *لَا أَعْرِفُ* I don't know.

tip.en: Three negatives, three times: *لَا* does not, *لَمْ* did not, *لَنْ* will not.

when.en: Saying something did not happen.

how.en: *لَمْ* takes the present, cut short (the jussive). The last vowel goes silent, and the endings *ـِينَ ـُونَ ـَانِ* lose their *ن*: *يَكْتُبُ* becomes *لَمْ يَكْتُبْ*, *يَكْتُبُونَ* becomes *لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا*. So *لَمْ* + present means past.

tip.en: *مَا* + past means the same and is common in speech: *مَا كَتَبْتُ*. The written standard prefers *لَمْ*.

when.en: Saying something will not happen.

how.en: *لَنْ* takes the present with a final *ـَ* (the subjunctive), and *ـِينَ ـُونَ* lose their *ن*: *لَنْ أَذْهَبَ* I will not go, *لَنْ يَذْهَبُوا* they will not go. No *سَ*.

ex.en: You won't find one like it. (to a woman)

tip.en: The same form follows *أَنْ* (to, that): *أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ* I want to go.

when.en: Habits in the past and things that were going on: when I was young I used to play; she was reading when I came.

how.en: Put the past of *كَانَ* before the present of the main verb. Both agree with the person: *كُنْتُ أَلْعَبُ* I used to play, *كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ* they were working.

ex.en: I used to live in Cairo.
She was reading when I arrived.

tip.en: *كَانَ* alone is was: *كَانَ الْجَوُّ جَمِيلًا* the weather was nice.

when.en: When the doer is unknown or unimportant: the door was opened, the book was written in 1990.

how.en: Same letters, new vowels. Past: u on the first letter, i before the last (*كَتَبَ* wrote, *كُتِبَ* was written). Present: u on the prefix, a before the last (*يَكْتُبُ*, *يُكْتَبُ*). It agrees with the thing acted on: *كُتِبَتِ الرِّسَالَةُ*.

ex.en: It is said that he is ill.

tip.en: In plain text the passive looks exactly like the active. That is why Ṭalāqa keeps its vowels on longer.

when.en: Arabic tells apart you to a man and you to a woman, and has a dual for two people.

how.en: Start with eight: *أَنَا* I, *أَنْتَ* you (m), *أَنْتِ* you (f), *هُوَ* he, *هِيَ* she, *نَحْنُ* we, *أَنْتُمْ* you all, *هُمْ* they. The feminine plurals *أَنْتُنَّ* and *هُنَّ* come at A2, the duals *أَنْتُمَا* and *هُمَا* at B1. Speech mostly uses the eight.

ex.en: Where are you from? (to a woman)

tip.en: Because the verb's prefix and ending show the person, the pronoun is often left out.

when.en: From B1. Most verbs fit one of ten patterns built on a three-letter root. Each pattern shifts the meaning in a regular way.

how.en: Form I is the plain verb. II often means make do (*عَلِمَ* knew, *عَلَّمَ* taught). III means do with someone (*كَاتَبَ* corresponded). V and VI are the reflexive and mutual of II and III (*تَعَلَّمَ* learnt, *تَكَاتَبَ* wrote to each other). VII is passive-like (*اِنْكَسَرَ* broke). VIII is often for oneself (*اِسْتَمَعَ* listened). X means ask for or consider (*اِسْتَخْدَمَ* used).

ex.en: I studied Arabic, and now I teach it.

tip.en: Grammarians write the patterns with the letters ف ع ل. Form IX (colours) is rare and left out.

when.en: When a root has *و* or *ي* (or a hamza, or a doubled letter), the verb bends. Many of the commonest verbs are like this.

how.en: Hollow (*و* or *ي* in the middle): *قَالَ*, *يَقُولُ*, but *قُلْتُ*: the long vowel shrinks when a consonant ending follows. Defective (at the end): *مَشَى*, *يَمْشِي*, *مَشَيْتُ*. Assimilated (*و* first): *وَصَلَ*, *يَصِلُ*, the *و* drops in the present. Doubled: *رَدَّ*, *رَدَدْتُ*.

tip.en: The drills use these on purpose. When a form looks odd, open the verb's table.

when.en: Printed in the Qurʾan, children's books and learner texts. Left out almost everywhere else.

how.en: *ـَ* fatḥa a, *ـِ* kasra i, *ـُ* ḍamma u, *ـْ* sukūn no vowel, *ـّ* shadda doubles the letter. Tanwīn *ـً ـٍ ـٌ* adds n. In Ṭalāqa a new word shows all its marks; after two right answers only the shadda stays; once you know it, none. Hold any word to see them again.

tip.en: When you type, the marks never count. Type the letters; the vowels are for reading.

when.en: Every time you say the: *ال* is joined to its word.

how.en: Before a moon letter the l is said: *الْقَمَر* al-qamar. Before a sun letter it melts and the letter doubles: *الشَّمْس* ash-shams. Sun letters: *ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن*. After a vowel, the a of al- drops too: *فِي الْبَيْتِ* fil-bayt.

tip.en: There is no word for a or an: *بَيْت* is a house.

when.en: Behind almost every word: three root letters carry a meaning; a pattern of vowels and extra letters makes the word.

how.en: *ك ت ب* is about writing: *كَتَبَ* wrote, *كَاتِب* writer, *كِتَاب* book, *مَكْتَب* office, desk, *مَكْتَبَة* library, *مَكْتُوب* written. Patterns repeat: *مَـ...ـَة* is often a place (*مَدْرَسَة* school, from *د ر س* study), *فَاعِل* the doer (*كَاتِب*, *لَاعِب* player).

ex.en: The writer is in the library.

tip.en: Dictionaries list words under their root. Spotting the root lets you guess words you have never seen.

when.en: Arabic has endings for some plurals and changes the inside of most others.

how.en: Sound plurals add an ending: *ـُونَ* (*ـِينَ* after a preposition or as an object) for men, *ـَات* for most feminine words (*مُعَلِّم* → *مُعَلِّمُونَ*, *سَيَّارَة* → *سَيَّارَات*). Broken plurals rearrange the vowels: *كِتَاب* → *كُتُب*, *بَيْت* → *بُيُوت*, *وَلَد* → *أَوْلَاد*. Learn each with its word. Two of anything is the dual: *كِتَابَانِ*.

tip.en: Plurals of things count as feminine singular: *الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ* the books are new (literally, it is new).

when.en: Every noun is one or the other, and adjectives and verbs agree with it.

how.en: Most words ending in *ة* are feminine. So are women, most countries and cities, and some body parts that come in pairs (*عَيْن*, *يَد*). Adjectives add *ة* for the feminine: *كَبِير*, *كَبِيرَة*. Verbs too: *هُوَ ذَهَبَ*, *هِيَ ذَهَبَتْ*.

tip.en: The adjective comes after the noun, and takes *ال* too when the noun has it: *الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ* the big house.

when.en: Saying what something is, now.

how.en: Put the two parts side by side: *أَنَا طَالِبٌ* I (am) a student, *الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ* the house (is) big. The first part has *ال*, the second does not; that gap is the is. In the past use *كَانَ*, and for not, *لَيْسَ*.

tip.en: To have is a preposition: *عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ* I have a car, literally at me (is) a car.

when.en: The door of the house, Cairo University, a cup of coffee.

how.en: Put the two nouns side by side: *بَابُ الْبَيْتِ* the door of the house. The first never takes *ال*, even though it means the; its *ة* is said t: *جَامِعَةُ الْقَاهِرَةِ* jāmiʿat al-qāhira.

tip.en: A possessive ending makes a word definite too: *كِتَابِي* my book, never *الْكِتَابِي*.

when.en: My book, with him, I saw her: the pronoun is an ending on the noun, preposition or verb.

how.en: *ـِي* my, *ـُكَ* your (m), *ـُكِ* your (f), *ـُهُ* his, *ـُهَا* her, *ـُنَا* our, *ـُكُمْ* your (pl), *ـُهُمْ* their. *ة* turns into *ت* before them: *سَيَّارَة* → *سَيَّارَتِي*. On a verb, me is *ـنِي*: *سَاعِدْنِي* help me.

ex.en: What is your name? (to a man)

tip.en: After *i* or *ī*, *ـهُ* becomes *ـهِ*: *فِيهِ* in it, *عَلَيْهِ* on him.

when.en: Counting things. Famous for being back to front.

how.en: One and two follow the noun like adjectives, or the noun's dual says it: *كِتَابٌ وَاحِدٌ*, *كِتَابَانِ*. From 3 to 10 the number takes the opposite gender to the noun, and the noun is plural: *ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ* (masculine noun, *ة* on the number), *ثَلَاثُ سَيَّارَاتٍ*. From 11 up the noun is singular: *عِشْرُونَ كِتَابًا*.

tip.en: Digits: ٠ ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩ in the East, 0 to 9 in North Africa. Numbers are written left to right even inside Arabic.

when.en: Fuṣḥā, Modern Standard Arabic, is written and heard on the news everywhere. At home, people speak their dialect.

how.en: Ṭalāqa teaches fuṣḥā for everything, and the ʿIbārāt tile adds the everyday phrases in two big dialects: shāmī (Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Palestine) and maṣrī (Egypt), understood across the Arab world from films and TV. Common differences: *مَاذَا* what is *شُو* in shāmī and *إِيه* in maṣrī; *أُرِيدُ* I want is *بَدِّي* and *عَايِز*; *قَ* is often said as a catch in the throat.

ex.en: I would like a coffee, please.

tip.en: Speak fuṣḥā to anyone and you will be understood; people may smile and answer in dialect.
